confidence.rationale: Major integrative reviews converge on dimensional reactivity and regulation, while theories differ in included dimensions, biological emphasis, age coverage, and boundaries with personality.

limitations: The definition does not establish one universally correct taxonomy, instrument, biological basis, or causal pathway.

scope.population: Humans studied from infancy through adulthood with age-appropriate temperament measures.
scope.temporal_scope: Repeated tendencies and regulation across situations and development rather than one isolated episode.

claims.statement: Contemporary temperament research describes multiple continuous dimensions of reactivity and self-regulation that show relative continuity while developing through biological and contextual influences; it is not a validated four-type classification of people.

confidence.rationale: The forms were developed with 468 parent reports and evaluated with 1,189 participants, but performance varied by scale and population and the very short model fit was marginal.

claims.confounding_note: Informant expectations, shared method, item selection, language, culture, socioeconomic conditions, age, missingness, and sample composition can influence the observed measurement properties.

estimate.metric: reliability, criterion validity, stability, agreement, and factor-model performance
estimate.notes: Most properties were satisfactory in mid- or high-income and White samples; some internal consistencies were lower in African American and low-income samples, and very short three-factor fit was marginal.

limitations: Questionnaire reliability and validity do not make the score a direct observation of temperament or prove the proposed three broad factors are universal.

boundary_conditions: The reported English-language CBQ forms, age range, caregiver respondents, samples, scoring, and psychometric analyses.
scope.population: Children aged 3 to 8 years represented in the CBQ short-form development and evaluation samples, predominantly mid- or high-income and White with additional African American and low-income samples.
scope.temporal_scope: Caregiver questionnaire administration and psychometric evaluation in the reported samples.

claims.statement: Putnam and Rothbart's CBQ short and very short forms showed useful internal consistency, criterion validity, longitudinal stability, and cross-informant agreement in the reported samples, with weaker properties for some scales and populations and only marginal three-factor fit for the very short form.

confidence.rationale: The quantitative review compiled 3,217 coefficients from 152 longitudinal studies, but heterogeneous traits, instruments, cohorts, and historical studies limit a single estimate for modern temperament dimensions.

claims.confounding_note: Measurement reliability and comparability, age, retest interval, attrition, cohort, construct breadth, informant, and sample restriction affect rank-order estimates.

estimate.metric: meta-analytic rank-order test-retest correlation at a 6.7-year interval
estimate.notes: Mean estimates increased from .31 in childhood to .54 in college years, .64 around age 30, and about .74 between ages 50 and 70; temperament dimensions were less consistent than adult personality traits.

limitations: Group-level rank-order consistency does not imply that an individual cannot change, that mean levels are stable, or that childhood measures determine adulthood.

boundary_conditions: The personality and temperament constructs, measures, ages, intervals, and cohorts included in the meta-analysis.
scope.population: Participants from childhood through older adulthood represented in 152 longitudinal personality and temperament studies.
scope.temporal_scope: Longitudinal retest intervals analyzed across the lifespan, standardized in reported age comparisons to 6.7 years.

claims.statement: In Roberts and DelVecchio's meta-analysis, rank-order consistency of measured personality and temperament traits was moderate rather than perfect, increased from childhood into adulthood, and decreased across longer retest intervals.

confidence.rationale: Repeated overlapping assessments provide unusually direct cross-age evidence, but one cultural cohort, measurement models, attrition, and observational design limit generalization and causal interpretation.

claims.confounding_note: Shared reporter or method, socioeconomic and cultural context, stable environments, measurement overlap, genetic influences, and unmeasured developmental experiences can contribute to continuity.

estimate.metric: longitudinal continuity between conceptually related temperament and Big Five dimensions
estimate.notes: The strongest relations occurred between conceptually similar traits; joint traits showed rank-order stability alongside mean-level changes.

limitations: The cohort does not establish universal pathways, immutable traits, or that effortful control causes broad personality maturation.

boundary_conditions: The cohort, measures, overlapping ages, latent growth models, retention, and historical context represented in Ringwald et al.
scope.population: 674 Mexican-origin youth in the reported longitudinal cohort.
scope.temporal_scope: Temperament assessments at ages 10 to 16 and Big Five personality assessments at ages 14 to 26.

claims.statement: In one longitudinal cohort of 674 Mexican-origin youth, measured temperament from ages 10 to 16 showed continuity with conceptually related Big Five personality dimensions through age 26 while also showing mean-level developmental change.

confidence.rationale: Behavior-genetic meta-analysis partitions sources of longitudinal covariance and reviews support transactional models, but variance decomposition does not identify concrete causal processes or their direction.

claims.falsifiable_boundary: The proposed account is weakened when repeated, independently measured person-environment processes add no explanatory or predictive value beyond measurement stability and when experimentally changed candidate processes do not alter prespecified later behavior.
limitations: Heritability, genetic stability, or environmental variance are population statistics and must not be treated as fixed causes within an individual.

boundary_conditions: Longitudinal designs with age-appropriate repeated measures and explicit genetic, environmental, maturational, relational, or learning variables.
scope.population: Humans represented in longitudinal temperament, personality, and behavioral-genetic studies.
scope.temporal_scope: Repeated development from infancy through adulthood.

claims.statement: Continuity and change in temperament and personality may emerge through repeated transactions among biologically influenced reactivity, developing regulation, relationships, learning, and increasingly stable environments.
claims.temporal_ordering: Earlier measured dispositions and environments precede later measurements, but reciprocal influence and stable confounding remain possible.

evidence.design: Multi-sample questionnaire development and evaluation using item analysis, internal consistency, criterion validity, longitudinal stability, cross-informant agreement, and confirmatory factor analysis.

effect.metric: psychometric performance of CBQ short and very short forms
effect.notes: Broadly satisfactory properties with lower internal consistency for some scales and populations and marginal three-factor fit for the very short form.

evidence.extraction_locator: PubMed abstract reporting form development, sample sizes, age range, internal consistency, criterion validity, stability, cross-informant agreement, population differences, and factor fit.
limitations: The instrument-development data do not establish cross-cultural invariance, equivalence to direct observation, or one universal temperament taxonomy.
evidence.population: 468 parents in form development and 1,189 participants in subsequent evaluation of children aged 3 to 8 years.
evidence.summary: The CBQ short forms reduced burden while retaining useful measurement properties in the reported samples, with explicit scale, model-fit, and population limitations.

evidence.design: Quantitative review of longitudinal test-retest rank-order consistency across childhood, adulthood, and old age.

effect.metric: rank-order test-retest correlation standardized to 6.7 years
effect.notes: Estimated consistency rose from .31 in childhood toward .74 at ages 50 to 70 and declined with longer intervals.

evidence.extraction_locator: PubMed abstract reporting 152 studies, 3,217 coefficients, age-standardized rank-order correlations, interval moderation, and lower consistency for temperament than adult personality traits.
limitations: Historical measures and heterogeneous constructs make the pooled estimates an indirect benchmark for any one contemporary temperament instrument.
evidence.population: Participants in 152 longitudinal personality and temperament studies across the lifespan.
evidence.summary: Trait rank ordering showed increasing but imperfect longitudinal consistency, contradicting both complete instability and immutable childhood typing.

evidence.design: Longitudinal cohort study with Rothbart-model temperament assessments from ages 10 to 16 and Big Five assessments from ages 14 to 26, including overlapping measures and joint latent growth models.

effect.metric: longitudinal continuity of conceptually related temperament and personality traits
effect.notes: Conceptually similar dimensions showed the strongest continuity while joint dimensions also changed in mean level.

evidence.extraction_locator: PubMed abstract reporting cohort size, ages, repeated overlapping temperament and Big Five measures, latent growth modeling, continuity, stability, and mean-level change.
limitations: One cohort and observational latent models cannot establish universal construct identity or causal maturation pathways.
evidence.population: 674 Mexican-origin youth followed from late childhood or adolescence into adulthood.
evidence.summary: Repeated overlapping measurement supported continuity between adolescent temperament and adult personality without eliminating developmental change.

evidence.design: Meta-analysis of longitudinal sibling and twin designs decomposing phenotypic personality stability into genetic and environmental covariance components across age.
evidence.extraction_locator: PubMed abstract reporting 24 longitudinal behavioral-genetic studies, 21,057 sibling pairs, and age trends in genetic and environmental contributions to personality stability.
limitations: Variance decomposition depends on behavioral-genetic assumptions and labels broad sources rather than measuring specific relationships, learning histories, roles, or environments.
evidence.population: 21,057 sibling pairs from six relationship types spanning infancy to old age in 24 longitudinal studies.
evidence.summary: Both genetic and environmental influences became more stable with age, while increasing environmental continuity contributed substantially to increasing phenotypic stability.

metadata.description: Separates temperament dimensions, momentary reactivity, effortful control, observed behavior, informant response, scale score, longitudinal stability, later personality, and proposed developmental processes.
metadata.title: Evidence pack for dimensional temperament and development

boundary_notes: Modern temperament models use multiple continuous dimensions rather than assigning every person to one of four classical types.
Relatively enduring does not mean fixed, context-free, purely biological, or immune to development.
Temperament overlaps with but is not identical to adult personality, current emotion, symptoms, diagnosis, or moral character.
objects.definition: Relatively enduring individual differences in emotional, motor, and attentional reactivity and in processes that regulate those reactions, studied as dimensions across development.
objects.label: Developmental temperament dimensions

boundary_notes: A negative-affectivity score is not a current negative emotion, diagnosis, or proof of future psychopathology.
objects.definition: Broad dimensional tendency toward more frequent or intense fear, frustration, sadness, discomfort, or difficulty recovering, as operationalized by a declared temperament model and measure.
objects.label: Temperamental negative affectivity

boundary_notes: Surgency is not identical to adult Extraversion, impulsivity, or observed activity in one situation.
objects.definition: Broad dimensional tendency involving activity, positive anticipation, high-intensity pleasure, sociability, or approach toward novelty and reward, as defined by a declared model and measure.
objects.label: Temperamental surgency and approach

boundary_notes: Effortful control is not a direct observation, one executive-function score, obedience, willpower, or moral worth.
Age, task demands, motivation, fatigue, instruction, opportunity, and environment can alter observed performance.
objects.definition: Dimensional capacity to direct attention and inhibit a dominant response or activate a subdominant response when doing so serves a current goal.
objects.label: Temperamental effortful control

boundary_notes: One reactive episode is evidence about behavior in that context, not the temperament dimension itself.
objects.definition: Time-indexed emotional, motor, orienting, or attentional response occurring when a person encounters a declared stimulus or situation.
objects.label: Context-specific reactive state

objects.definition: Observable approach, withdrawal, vocalization, motor activity, gaze, delay, inhibition, or attentional shift coded in a declared temperament-eliciting situation.
objects.function_note: Similar behavior can reflect temperament, learning, skill, current state, relationship, task understanding, or situational demand.
objects.label: Observed temperament-relevant response
objects.response_topography: Protocol-defined emotional, motor, or attentional response coded during a structured or naturalistic observation.

boundary_notes: A caregiver report integrates observations across settings but also depends on memory, interpretation, expectations, reference group, and response style.
objects.definition: Questionnaire context in which a caregiver rates a child's recent behavior in specified everyday situations using a version of the Children's Behavior Questionnaire.

dimensions.reference: frequency or typicality of described behavior
dimensions.target_age: 3 to 8 years in the Putnam and Rothbart short-form study

objects.label: CBQ caregiver-report assessment
objects.scope: CBQ administration and scoring within populations, languages, ages, and forms for which measurement properties have been evaluated.

objects.definition: Observable selection of a questionnaire response describing how often or how typically a child showed a specified behavior in a specified class of situations.
objects.function_note: The rating is the informant's response and is not the child's temperament dimension itself.
objects.label: Caregiver temperament item rating
objects.response_topography: Selection of one protocol-defined response option for a CBQ item.

boundary_notes: Scores depend on form, items, informant, age, language, population, and scoring model.
The very short form trades detail for burden and showed only marginal fit to a three-factor model in the cited development study.
objects.definition: Scored profile derived from caregiver item ratings, estimating fine-grained scales or broad factors such as Negative Affectivity, Surgency or Extraversion, and Effortful Control under a declared CBQ form.
objects.label: CBQ temperament dimension profile
objects.method: Use the selected CBQ form, scoring key, language, age range, missing-data rules, and informant identity; report scale-level reliability and validity for the relevant population.

boundary_notes: Observation samples fewer situations than caregiver report and the two methods should not be assumed interchangeable.
objects.definition: Protocol-based coding or task score derived from directly observed responses in situations selected to elicit temperament-relevant variation.
objects.label: Structured temperament observation
objects.method: Record declared stimuli, setting, coder training, response windows, reliability, and aggregation across tasks and occasions.

objects.definition: Repeated assessment context in which comparable temperament or personality dimensions are measured across multiple ages to estimate continuity and change.

dimensions.outcomes: rank-order stability, mean-level change, or cross-domain continuity

objects.label: Longitudinal temperament-personality assessment
objects.scope: Longitudinal designs represented by the included meta-analyses and cohort study.

boundary_notes: Relative standing is sample- and measure-dependent and is not a fixed identity or causal endpoint.
objects.definition: A person's estimated relative position on a later age-appropriate personality dimension in a declared longitudinal analysis.
objects.label: Later personality trait standing

boundary_notes: Rank-order stability does not mean no individual changes or that the group mean is unchanged.
A longitudinal association does not by itself identify genetic, maturational, relational, or environmental causes.
objects.definition: Statistical estimate of rank-order continuity or cross-age association between declared temperament or personality measurements.
objects.label: Longitudinal trait stability estimate
objects.method: Estimate age-, interval-, measure-, and sample-specific longitudinal associations while reporting attrition, measurement comparability, and uncertainty.

boundary_notes: Statistical genetic or environmental variance components do not identify a concrete developmental mechanism.
The model permits reciprocal and nonlinear change and does not imply that early temperament determines adult personality.
objects.definition: Proposed process in which biologically influenced reactivity and regulation repeatedly interact with maturation, relationships, learning, roles, and environments, producing both continuity and change in later personality-relevant behavior.
objects.label: Developmental temperament transaction
realization_conditions: Temperament-relevant responses and environments are measured repeatedly rather than reconstructed from one adult report.
Measurement invariance and age-appropriate construct continuity are evaluated.
Genetic, maturational, learning, relationship, and broader environmental alternatives are compared rather than collapsed.

sources.authority_note: Multi-author integrative review used to frame convergence and continuing disagreements among modern temperament approaches.
sources.title: What is temperament now? Assessing progress in temperament research on the twenty-fifth anniversary of Goldsmith et al.

sources.authority_note: Recent review used for current framing of infant reactivity, self-regulation, measurement diversity, development, context, and remaining reproducibility gaps.
sources.title: Temperament development in infancy — what we have learned about the origins of individual differences in the past 25 years

sources.authority_note: Primary instrument-development report used for CBQ scope, scoring levels, sample limitations, and measurement properties.
sources.title: Development of short and very short forms of the Children's Behavior Questionnaire

sources.authority_note: Large lifespan meta-analysis used specifically to distinguish relative rank-order stability from immutability.
sources.title: The rank-order consistency of personality traits from childhood to old age — a quantitative review of longitudinal studies

sources.authority_note: Recent longitudinal cohort with overlapping temperament and Big Five measurement, used with narrow population and noncausal scope.
sources.title: Linking temperament and personality traits from late childhood to adulthood by examining continuity, stability, and change

sources.authority_note: Behavioral-genetic meta-analysis used as indirect evidence constraining, not proving, developmental transaction mechanisms.
sources.title: Genetic and environmental continuity in personality development — a meta-analysis
